b: Dog is one of English's great etymological mysteries. It appears in late Old English as docga, probably first for a particular breed, while the usual word was hund (hound). Linguists still don't know where docga came from.

q.p: Do we know where the word 'dog' comes from?

rq.p: What was the usual Old English word for dog?

why: Some words appear without a clear ancestor.

b: Swapping the first sounds of words, like 'a blushing crow' for 'a crushing blow', is called a spoonerism. It's named after William Archibald Spooner, an Oxford don famous for such slips, though many quotes attributed to him were invented by students.

q.p: What is a spoonerism?
o: Swapping the first sounds of words

rq.p: Who are spoonerisms named after?

why: The brain sometimes plans sounds ahead and mixes them up.

b: A palindrome reads the same backwards and forwards, ignoring spaces and punctuation. Classics include 'racecar' and 'A man, a plan, a canal: Panama'. The word comes from the Greek palindromos, running back again.

q.p: Which of these is a palindrome?
o: A man, a plan, a canal: Panama
To be or not to be

rq.p: What does the Greek root of 'palindrome' mean?

why: Its letters mirror around the centre.

b: The claim that Inuit languages have dozens of words for snow is misleading. These languages build long words from many parts, so one root can make endless forms. By that counting, English has many snow words too: slush, sleet, powder, blizzard, drift.

q.p: Who is cappuccino named after?

why: The milky coffee matched their robes.

q.p: Did 'posh' come from 'port out, starboard home'?

rq.p: Is the real origin of 'posh' known?

why: Acronym origins for old words are almost always invented.

t: 'Rule of thumb' isn't about beating wives
b: A story claims old English law allowed a man to beat his wife with a stick no thicker than his thumb. Historians have found no such law. The phrase most likely comes from using your thumb as a rough measuring tool.

q.p: Did 'rule of thumb' come from a law about beating?
o: No, there's no evidence of such a law
It came from carpentry rules only

o: Using the thumb to measure roughly

why: An inch was once roughly a thumb's width.

b: In Plato's allegory, prisoners chained in a cave see only shadows on a wall and think they're reality. One escapes, sees the real world in sunlight, and returns to tell the others, who don't believe him. It's about education and how we know what's real.

q.p: In Plato's cave, what do the prisoners mistake for reality?

b: The Greek philosopher Diogenes rejected comfort and convention, reportedly living in a large ceramic jar in Athens. When Alexander the Great offered him any favour, Diogenes is said to have asked him to stand out of his sunlight.

o: To stand out of his sunlight

rq.p: Where did Diogenes reportedly live?

why: He believed needing little made you free.

t: Confucius's version of the golden rule
b: Long before many later versions, Confucius taught: 'Do not impose on others what you do not wish for yourself.' Similar principles appear across many religions and philosophies worldwide.

q.p: What did Confucius say about treating others?
o: Don't do to others what you wouldn't want

rq.p: Is the golden rule unique to one culture?

why: Empathy-based ethics arose independently in many places.

b: Around 343 BC, King Philip II of Macedon hired the philosopher Aristotle to tutor his 13-year-old son, the future Alexander the Great. He taught him for several years, covering subjects from ethics to medicine.

q.p: Who tutored the young Alexander the Great?

why: Philip wanted the best mind in Greece for his heir.

b: Philosopher Immanuel Kant lived his whole life in and around Königsberg. He was so regular in his habits that, according to a popular story, neighbours could set their clocks by his afternoon walk.

why: Strict routine left his mind free for hard thinking.

t: The 'Mozart effect' is mostly a myth
b: A 1993 study found students did slightly better on a spatial task right after hearing Mozart. It was hyped as 'Mozart makes babies smarter'. Later research found the small effect was short-lived, and likely came from music lifting mood and alertness.

q.p: Does listening to Mozart make you smarter long-term?

why: Any enjoyable music had similar effects in later studies.

t: The pangram that uses every letter
b: 'The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog' contains every letter of the English alphabet. Sentences like this, called pangrams, were used to test typewriters and to show off fonts.

q.p: Why did Galileo publish a discovery as an anagram?

t: Hello took off with the telephone
b: Hello existed before phones, but it was mainly used to attract attention or express surprise. Thomas Edison championed it as the standard way to answer the telephone in the late 1870s. Alexander Graham Bell preferred 'ahoy'.

q.p: What did Alexander Graham Bell want people to say when answering the phone?

rq.p: Who championed 'hello' for the phone?

why: Edison's choice spread with telephone exchanges.

why: 'Octo' refers to its eight ends.
